title: Maynard Company (A): building balance sheets from account balances
summary: Case 2-1: sort the Exhibit 1 balances into balance sheets at June 1 and June 30, compare the two, and see why retained earnings rose by less than net income.

chunks.heading: The case: a bookkeeper quits
chunks.explanation_md:
**Case 2-1, Maynard Company (A)**. **Diane Maynard** owns all the stock of **Maynard Company**. Her bookkeeper has quit, leaving a book with the numbers already entered. She asks a friend to prepare **balance sheets** and comment on the numbers. She mentions two things: the **Cash account is healthy**, and **net income in June was $19,635**.

The friend copies the account balances at the **start and end of June** into **Exhibit 1**. One more fact: at the **end of June** Diane Maynard **paid herself an $11,700 dividend** and used that money to **repay her loan from the company**.

The four questions: (1) prepare balance sheets as of **June 1** and **June 30**; (2) comment on how the financial condition changed; (3) explain why **retained earnings did not rise by the full June net income**; (4) is the company **worth the Shareholder's Equity of $619,446**?
chunks.exam_line: Maynard (A): net income $19,635 in June; an $11,700 dividend was used to repay Diane Maynard's loan from the company; equity at June 30 is $619,446.

chunks.heading: Sorting Exhibit 1 into assets, liabilities and equity
chunks.explanation_md:
Exhibit 1 lists the accounts **alphabetically**, mixed together. The first job is to sort them.

**Assets:** Cash; Accounts receivable; Note receivable, Diane Maynard; Merchandise inventory; Prepaid insurance; Supplies on hand; Building; Equipment (at cost); Land; Other noncurrent assets.

**Deducted from assets:** Accumulated depreciation on building, and accumulated depreciation on equipment. These are shown as **minus** figures under Building and Equipment, so each asset appears at its cost less accumulated depreciation.

**Liabilities:** Accounts payable; Accrued wages payable; Bank notes payable; Taxes payable; Other noncurrent liabilities.

**Shareholder's equity:** Capital stock and Retained earnings.

key_terms.meaning: The owner's loan from the company, an asset of the company until she repays it.

chunks.explanation_md:

**Comparing the two dates:**
- Total assets rose by **$43,350**, but liabilities rose by **$35,415** and equity by only **$7,935**.

So most of the growth in assets was funded by more borrowing and more unpaid bills, not by equity.

chunks.heading: Why retained earnings rose by less than net income
chunks.explanation_md:
Net income was **$19,635**, yet retained earnings went from **$221,511** to only **$229,446**. Why?

Because of the **$11,700 dividend** Diane Maynard paid herself at the end of June. Net income adds to retained earnings; the dividend takes money out of them:

221,511 + 19,635 = 241,146
241,146 minus 11,700 = **229,446**

So equity rose by only **$7,935** (19,635 minus 11,700). And because she used the dividend to repay her loan, the note receivable fell from $11,700 to zero.

**Is the company worth $619,446?** That figure is capital stock **$390,000** plus retained earnings **$229,446**. It is the **residual interest**: total assets of $681,888 minus total liabilities of $62,442, as recorded in the company's books.
chunks.exam_line: Retained earnings: 221,511 + net income 19,635 minus dividend 11,700 = 229,446. Shareholder's Equity $619,446 = capital stock + retained earnings = assets minus liabilities in the books.

questions.stem: Maynard's net income for June was $19,635, yet retained earnings rose only from $221,511 to $229,446. Explain why, with working.
questions.model_answer_md:
Retained earnings go up by net income and down by dividends, and Maynard paid a dividend in June.

**Working**
- Opening retained earnings: **221,511**
- Add net income for June: 221,511 + 19,635 = **241,146**
- Less the **$11,700 dividend** Diane Maynard paid herself at the end of June: 241,146 - 11,700 = **229,446**

So retained earnings, and equity, rose by only 19,635 - 11,700 = **7,935**.

**Where the dividend went:** she used it to repay her loan from the company, so the note receivable from Diane Maynard fell from 11,700 to zero.

**Conclusion:** net income adds to retained earnings but the dividend takes money out, so the rise is net income minus dividends.

rubric.point: Net income adds to retained earnings: 221,511 + 19,635 = 241,146
Dividend of 11,700 reduces retained earnings
Equity rose only 7,935; dividend used to repay her note

questions.model_answer_md:

|---|---|

questions.stem: As of June 30, is Maynard Company worth the amount shown in Shareholder's Equity, $619,446? Explain.
questions.model_answer_md:
This is the fourth question of the Maynard (A) case.

- **What the figure is:** capital stock **390,000** + retained earnings **229,446** = **619,446**.
- It equals **total assets 681,888 minus total liabilities 62,442**, the **residual interest**.
- Those amounts are the balances **recorded in the company's books** (for example, the building at its cost less accumulated depreciation).

So $619,446 is a book figure for the owner's claim, not a separate measure of what the company is worth.

**Conclusion:** shareholder's equity tells us the residual interest as recorded, not necessarily what the company is worth.

rubric.point: 619,446 = capital stock 390,000 + retained earnings 229,446
Equals assets 681,888 minus liabilities 62,442: residual interest
Based on amounts recorded in the books

questions.stem: Comment on how Maynard Company's financial condition at the end of June compared with the beginning of June. Diane Maynard says the Cash account is healthy: is that the whole story?
questions.model_answer_md:
Comparing the two balance sheets shows where the growth in June came from.

**Headline changes ($)**

| Item | June 1 | June 30 | Change |
|---|---|---|---|
| Total assets | 638,538 | 681,888 | +43,350 |
| Total liabilities | 27,027 | 62,442 | +35,415 |
| Shareholder's equity | 611,511 | 619,446 | +7,935 |

**What drove them**
- **Cash** rose from 34,983 to 66,660, up **31,677**, so Diane Maynard is right that cash looks healthy.
- But **bank notes payable** rose from 8,385 to 29,250 (up **20,865**, more than tripled) and **accounts payable** from 8,517 to 21,315 (up **12,798**).
- **Equipment at cost** rose by **23,400** (13,260 to 36,660).
- The **note receivable** from Diane Maynard of 11,700 is gone because she repaid it with her dividend.
- **Equity** rose by only 7,935: net income of 19,635 less the 11,700 dividend.

**Comment**
- Most of the growth in assets was funded by **more borrowing and more unpaid bills**, not by equity.
- Liabilities more than doubled, so the company owes much more at the end of June than at the start.
- The higher cash balance is partly borrowed money, so cash alone does not show the full picture.

**Conclusion:** the company grew in June, but mainly on the back of liabilities; the healthy cash balance must be read together with the rise in bank notes and payables.

rubric.point: Assets up 43,350; liabilities up 35,415; equity up 7,935
Bank notes up 20,865 and accounts payable up 12,798
Equipment up 23,400; owner's note repaid
Growth funded mostly by borrowing and unpaid bills, not equity
Healthy cash partly borrowed: cash alone is not the full story
